review:
[h1] Story and Characters [/h1]

While playing this game, I felt like I was inside a Fast & Furious movie. I mean this in a good way because it has a fun story. The plot generally revolves around Tyler, who wants revenge. We also shouldn't forget Mac and Jess, who help our main character, Tyler. I mean, of course there is a story, but it is not legendary like the stories in the old NFS games. In my opinion, one of the things that made old NFS stories so strong was how easily we connected with the game. The presentation + atmosphere supported the story very well. Eddie's Skyline from NFS Underground is in this game, which is a nice and subtle detail. EA actually knows the value of its old games, but for some reason, they just never bring a REMAKE to the old ones... The story is good and sufficient, but it might not satisfy those expecting something truly great. Fortunately, where the story falls short, the mechanics support the gameplay.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3691389994
[h1] Gameplay and Mechanics [/h1]

One of the strongest sides of the game is customization and variety. It proves once again that it is the best of this genre when it comes to the abundance of cars and customization options. There are tons of licensed kits like Liberty Walk, Rocket Bunny, LOMA, and RTR. Another strong side of the game is the mechanics. Especially the drift mechanics took me back to the Carbon days. It has an extremely smooth and enjoyable mechanic. The only annoying part here is the non-destructible environment despite having such mechanics. Crashing into poles that you expect to break down hurts a bit. Especially not even being able to drive onto some curbs felt ridiculous.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3683940727
The class system was a good idea. Due to missions, the Runner class uses heavier armored vehicles and takes turns harder. The Rally and Drift classes are perfect for more precise and fast reflexes. Drag class cars do not turn at all :d As the name suggests, they are for drag races, but sometimes missions require us to drive 4-5 miles with drag cars. By the way, bringing back the DRAG races from the old games was very good. Although the races have plenty of content, after a point, they start repeating themselves and get boring. If you ask me, the biggest reason for this is the runner missions. In silly missions where we deliver packages or gather intel, very little time is given and we constantly have to drive while checking the map. After a while, it starts to get extremely boring. Lastly, earning money, customization, and performance parts through the Shipment mechanic and mini-events on the map was sensible and enjoyable.

[h1] Graphics and Atmosphere [/h1]

The game's map is large and successful. From deserts to the city center, it offers a great visual feast. With neon lights in night races and all... it took me back to NFSU2. I didn't see any issues with the game's optimization. While playing on 4K Ultra settings, I didn't experience any drops or anything. The atmosphere was sufficient for the story. I think many of us already know this game from the Mustang scene. Missions in that style made the gameplay much more fun.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3683954947
[h1] Overall [/h1]

A successful title that combines the series' core passion for customization with modern action. Even though it gets repetitive at some points, it makes up for this flaw with its enjoyable driving feel and atmosphere. It holds a little bit of the old NFS spirit inside. If only the old ones would get a REMAKE or REMASTER...

Buy in-game currency, with which you buy "booster packs", in which you could get some exchangeable cards, 3 of which you can use on a slot-like game to get a random card that might be better than the one you have and might be fitting your build.
Disapprove.

[h1]Great gameplay inside a cringefest! (Don't worry, it's a solid game!)[/h1]

Okay, i will start this by mentioning, i played NFS series since the first one, obviously, i got old and boomery so after Most Wanted (2005) came out i got disappointed, and ever since, NFS games stopped being one of my favourite franchises.
Anyhow, few days ago i caught this on a -90% sale, for 3$ i couldn't turn it down, i gave it a try thinkig "Ey, what the hell, let's see what's new".

And that's when i became a junkie.

In just few days i managed to play like 53 hours almost. I got hooked up on it like crazy.

My complaints are related mostly to the extra challenges (speedruns, drift challenges, jumps), if you want to get all the achievements/completely finish the game you have to do those, they're hell on earth. I would gladly spend 3 days in a jail instead of doing them. I am not a very good player (in my recent years i becamme a filthy casual), but still, they're just badly designed with big requirements.
I am almost certain the devs haven't done them themselves to see if they're even remotely feasible. And i read that previously, devs that worked on NFS series said that they were kinda forced into just releasing the games, and not polish them accordingly, i don't know if that's the case but i think it's likely.

Now, most people don't care about achievements or extra completion bullshit, i like to call them 'the happy ones'.

Another thing that kinda bugs me is that, it's a street racing game, right? Then why the hell do we have to go through so many checkpoints, it kinda beats the "street racing" vibe when you have to do things accordingly, there are just few shortcuts that aren't really shortcuts, you can easily miss these checkpoints, and you have to go back to them, which obviously, is as stupid as it sounds.

Story is a cringefest to say the least, i swear to God, it's like 2002 called and wanted Vin Diesel from XXX back. 
All the dialogues and pseudo-machoism you'd expect from that movie, or from the Fast and Furious series. 

It didn't bother me, though, it was so bad it was funny as hell.
Luckily, it's NFS. Nobody in this damn world that plays it gives a quarter of a fuck about the story.

Overall, the game is really solid, graphics are good, it just feels right playing it, cars don't have that sluggish wanna-be racing sim feeling.
I would definitely recommend people to play it, especially old-farts (I am not even that old, but sometimes i feel like it..) like me that got to the point they're too boomery to enjoy "modern" games anymore.

Gameplay: 8/10
Graphics: 7/10
Story: Vin Diesel/10

For the people that don't feel like reading an entire review, i will make few short points:

The bad:
- The extra challenges for achievements are awfully bad, tiring and too much
- Multiplayer is almost dead, at least on Ranked, not sure about the casual
- Checkpoints in races, and no "real" shortcuts
- Sometimes, slow loading screens even on a good computer where the game is also installed on the SSD

The good:
- If you pay attention to dialogues and cutscenes, you will feel the power of Great Van Diesel the 1st flow through you, you will hear Britney Spears in your head and a Nokia 3310 will spawn in your hand.
- I think there are lots of cars, that will appeal to every sort of category of people. You can even make Ted Bundy's beetle, or if you didn't have luck trading crypto or stocks the last few years, you can at least get a lambo in NFS.
- Lots of customizations (I wish there were more options when placing decals, to alter their shape only horizontally for example)
- Solid handling and feel when driving. It feels like NFS again, it's almost perfect.
- Plenty of stuff to do in free-roam
- It has a pretty easy learning/getting-used-to curve

I really enjoyed my time with this game, and i hope you will too!
Have a great day and thanks for reading my ramblings.

A small edit: I forgot to mention, Payback really brought back my love for racing games, so now i am installing a bunch of racing games i already own for when i have time to play.

I wish I could recommend this game, I really do, but it has so many problems and it's quite sad to see the path it took

Pros:
-Quite a list of cars
-Customisation is nice
-The map is ok/good
-Characters are okay, could be better, but are passable
-Quite aggresive cops
-Songs that play depending on where you are and time of day (desert, downtown, mountain, etc. Morning, Afternoon, Night) Which is pretty creative

Neutral:
-The story could be better but it's nothing horrific in my eyes, It didn't gave me much of a sense to, well, Payback, since the start felt rushed, but at the final race I really got that feeling of bringing down The House

Cons:
-Optimiziation problems, it suffers from Watch Dogs 2 Syndrome where it lags even when in low graphics when there is a lot going on on the screen like cop chases and driving around the city, however it's better than Watch Dogs 2, since you don't get much lag on open areas, different from Watch Dogs 2 which is pretty much everywhere
-No free roaming cops, only for some events
-The AI can be a bit too punishing
-Not having the ability to change your handling settings like the 2015 game did, which can be quite annoying
-Airtime is a mechanic. Too much of it? Good luck getting collectibles cuz you will fly past them, or go way too high during a race and land where you didn't want to
-The way you get upgrades... It's basically The Crew 1's way of getting upgrades, you finish a race, you get a CARD that upgrades your engine/ecu/transmisison/whatever, and it's all very RPG-like, which isn't a good thing, you basically have to wait for the performance shop to restock so you can buy better parts, you can't just go there and buy the best ones in case you have the money
-Lootboxes, of course, why not, it's an EA game after all. Everyone wanted neon lights for their cars but they didn't deliver it on the 2015 game, everyone complained about it, so they added it! IN. MOTHER. F-CKING. LOOT BOXES. You basically have to open shipment crates to get a chance to get neon lights, which include colors and patterns in which they flash, along with nitrous colour, tire smoke, and horn sound, which is all cool and games until you realise you need to open lootboxes for them instead of just buying them. And the best part is? You use one of those items in your car, you can't take them off, to your inventory, you either delete them or replace them, you want to take it out and use in another car? Too bad, open more lootboxes so MAYBE you get the same neon/smoke/nitrous/horn. I bought the Deluxe Edition and I got 5 platinum neons, tire smokes, and nitrouses for free, which seemed pretty good until I realized I couldn't use them as much as I wanted because there are only 5 of each, if I use all of them, they're gone, like, forever. Such bullshit
-The deluxe edition doesn't come with the car pack dlc. Sure, I don't care much about those cars but, seriously? The D E L U X E edition doesn't come with all dlc? What a dissapointment

Conclusion:
6/10 - Need for Speed: Payback is a flawed game, it seemed to have potential, but was ruined by corporate greed. The story was okay, but enjoyable I guess. The songs were enjoyable. The car variety was enjoyable. The customization was enjoyable. Taking down The House was enjoyable. There are a couple of things in this game that make me believe that Ghost Games at least tried to deliver something decent, and it's quite unfortunate that EA had to ruin it all with microtransactions. I'm not gonna put all of the blame on EA however, some things in the game are probably Ghost's own fault, but still, the fact that this game has loot boxes, and when everyone wanted neon, they put neon in said loot boxes, shows what kind of company EA is.

If you want to buy the game, wait for a sale, and try it, if you like it, then that's very good, it's not the best game in the world, and I believe it's deserving of a downvote because of EA's incompetence, but it's worth giving a try at least for me, you might get some fun out of it. I'm glad that the next game, Need for Speed Heat, is better than this one in every aspect, It's too expensive for me to buy it since I live in Brazil, a harsh country with a shitty economy, but I hope I get the chance to play it one day. For now, Payback is the most recent need for speed I have, and although it is far from perfect, I cannot lie, it was a fun ride.

First off - I bought this on sale. If that wasn't the case, I would have a harder time recommending it. It has it's flaws, of course, but if you can live with the following:

- you will crash and take wrong turns every once in a while because you cannot spot the correct course in time (can restart/replay all events, though)
- the upgrade system is like a collectible card game for each car in contrast to common unlock-and-purchase- mechanics
- traffic will randomly ruin your attempts in driftzones, speedtraps and the like more often than not

then it is worth checking out!

In fact, there are a lot of things that I enjoy more than in NFS Heat.

- drifting is still not great, but a lot better than the abysmal NFS Heat variant
- you have a crew of 3 characters, each with their own specialties and cars for specific events
- 6 chapters of story with a good amount of races to them that require you play each of the characters
- story is good enough, and your characters actually have dialog and make comments in races
- opposing crews and their bossed try so hard to be mean and badass, it's already funny
- treasure hunting for 5 different wrecks that you can upgrade to very cool, outrageous builds
- a diverse landscape, from high speed desert roads and dusty offroad trails over serpentine mountain roads and villages to a city with bridges and tunnels - it is all there!
- lots of skill activities, collectibles and side duels against cops and street racers that you can do to earn resources but are not required since they don't contain unique rewards - you can earn all the stuff by doing the things you like.

If you like NFS in general and can get this on sale, you can't go wrong. The DLC cars are not that interesting and surely not required, purchse only if you have money to burn.
The map is pure robbery, don't support EA's moneygrubbing tactics. Unless you are an obsessive completionist, it is not necessary to find everything. There is no unique car or other unlock to be had that way.

Have fun!

You might be surprised to hear that there have already been 24 different 'Need for Speed' games. And while not all titles have appealed to all players, there have been some real hits. Hot Pursuit (2010) and Most Wanted (2005) were two of my most played games ever.

Need for Speed Payback received mixed ratings from the press but very positive feedback from players. In the end, it's always a matter of taste. Personally, I enjoyed this game very much and I highly recommend playing it.

The game has a very good story, beautiful graphics, many different cars, an interesting upgrade system, many events, and tons of side activities.

Based on the story you play with three different characters in different race styles.

Tyler "Ty" Morgan
Style: Racer, Drag

Style: Offroad, Drift, Speedcross

Jessica "Jess" Miller
Style: Runner
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2229909802
At release time many press reviews complained about micro-transactions. Yep, they exist, but you really don't need them at all. Steam sells the Deluxe Edition that already contains all the essential extra content like the 'Platinum Car Pack', the 'High Roller Pack' and the 'Speedcross Story Bundle'. Except for James Bonds old  Aston Martin DB5 you are going to miss nothing.

The second point people complain about is the upgrade system. You need cards to upgrade cars. There are six different types of cards, for specific mechanical bits. Head, block, ECU, turbo, exhaust, and transmission are areas you can upgrade. Additionally, cards offer special perks like acceleration, brakes, jump, nitrous, or speed. 

Cards can be bought in tuning shops and can also be generated randomly with a slot machine that you can run with tokens you earn after winning races. Yes, it's a little weird but really nothing to be upset about. Personally, I consider the upgrade system a fun aspect of the game. You can decide which cards you wish to buy and using the slot machine often rewards you with great cards that contain several perks.

As in many other modern racing games, you can collect vintage car parts in order to construct new cars and drive them. Finding car parts in 'Need for Speed Payback' is not a problem but collecting them is. In many cases, they seem impossible to reach. You often have to find nearby hills that you can jump off in order to reach the car part. At times, this can be a little annoying.

The game strongly concentrates on single-player. Unfortunately, multi-player is dead but except for the two achievements you have to collect in multiplayer, I didn't miss it at all.

The difficulty in Need for Speed Payback is well balanced. Normal difficulty is designed for the casual player and felt a little too easy in many events. But all the side activities are quite challenging and if you really want to beat all the speed traps, jumps, speed runs, drift zones, and roaming racers you need the right cars to succeed.

[h3][b]6/10 – Fun but forgettable[/b][/h3]

Being a big fan of the Need for Speed series since Hot Pursuit 2, I was heavily disappointed in releases like 2012's Most Wanted and 2013's Rivals, being one of the worst games released in the entire franchise to date in my opinion. 2015 was a step in the right direction but felt lacking when it came to the driving model. Having come off that, how does Need for Speed: Payback fare?

For those who want the short version - do I recommend it? Keeping in mind the horrible requirement of Origin & possibly bad optimization of the game, despite that I had a very enjoyable time with the game. So if you want a fun racing game you can spend, give or take, 10-ish hours as a first playthrough beating, I'd say go for it.

For those who want something a little extra - read on!

[h1]Story:[/h1]
NFS Payback's story isn't anywhere near as bad as some have made it out to be. Granted I don't think the pacing or writing of it was good but that doesn't mean I think it was bad. Rather I'd say it's underdeveloped instead. You go from being pals with Lina Navarro at the start to suddenly having her be your mortal enemy all within 20 minutes of the game and that just felt weird. They didn't give us enough time to invest into her character and give us a motive for hating her, it just felt like "lina do bad, you must go hate lina and take her down now" and that's about it.

I also think the main antagonists - The House - were left way too ambiguous. Not in a good way - they just didn't feel super significant in the grand scheme of things which is odd. Instead, what I end up remembering more about the story of Payback is probably the main trio you play as - Tyler, Mac and Jess - and the crews you take down along the way. But The House? I couldn't give two hoots about them as I played through and even after finishing them off in the last race I'm left wondering "who were they anyway?"

Where the game picks up the slack though I think is in the minor interactions & references. There were moments throughout the story where I had a giggle at some of the references to past games. I won't spoil them if you haven't seen them already yet but Payback likes to make callbacks to older NFS games and I thought that was a nice touch, even going on to answer some things about the older games. And the interactions your characters have with some of the crews you end up taking down are also entertaining, some just being smug, others feeling like the characters have a broken marriage among them where they hate each other one race and the next one they're all buddy-buddy reminiscing about their past. I found that really endearing.

[h1]Gameplay:[/h1]
Coming off of 2015's poorly-received driving model, Payback had a lot of shoes to fill. I'm very happy to report that the driving model is vastly improved over its predecessor's, making you feel like you have full control over your car...for the most part. Brake-to-drift is, once again, one of the main ways to get your car around corners, meaning it's still got that bootleg Burnout feeling to it. Admittedly it stopped bothering me after the first chapter of the game though I'm still not a huge fan of the way Need for Speed's been for the last 11+ years and sadly Payback is here to continue that trend. Despite that - the game feels great to play. Cars are fast, responsive and, baring in mind a few exceptions, I felt like I was actually in total control over my car. Getting from place to place, unlike in 2015, didn't feel like a chore and I greatly appreciate the improvements.

The one problem I have with the driving model in Payback is one of its core new introductions - off-roading. Off-roading honestly sometimes feels like the game has gone back to 2015 with cars being slippery and unresponsive. I get that it's the whole point - it's intended to be a challenge, but more often than not driving off-road meant it was time to wrestle with the game instead of actually playing it. The off-road races are going to be the closest thing to the "Tandem Drift" event from 2015 if you ever found that fun.

Improved driving model aside, there is one thing about the gameplay that I genuinely disliked and was a very common complaint throughout my playthrough - the progression system. Why oh WHY did they make the progression system based on GAMBLING?! I get it - it fits thematically with the game's lore. But is it fun to play? Hell no. GAMBLING for car upgrades is STUPID. Not being able to buy the parts you want for your build is STUPID. Having the upgrade shop be based on a timer is STUPID. The way you progress in this game is just STUPID. It is easily the worst part about the game and sours the experience for me. Sure you can earn Speed Cards by winning events, but if your car is underpowered for a specific part of the game and you wanna make it better - that's when you have to engage with this game's gambling & loot box system and it's DUMB. I genuinely hate it.

One minor comment I'm not sure whether I like or not is the lack of free roam cops. One the one hand - it makes traversing the open world to get to your next destination a lot smoother since you don't have to worry about getting randomly chased out of nowhere and the game has more than enough free roam activities to keep you busy & wandering around otherwise. On the other hand - for how involved the police is in the game's story it feels incredibly weird to leave them out of being able to chase you in free roam? Gotta take the good with the bad on this one I suppose. Personally despite how weird it is to not have them in free roam I didn't really mind all that much. The game filled in the cops' shoes well enough by giving you a huge variety of activities to partake in anyway.

[h1]Graphics, Sound & Optimization[/h1]
Despite playing the game entirely on low settings, I think NFS Payback looks great. It's visually distinct, vivid and disregarding the desert setting the game generally looks colorful, lively and full of detail. Cars get realistically dirty & damaged the more you drive & beat them and provides you with plenty of customization options for stuff like tire smoke & nitrous.

The music I can't comment on despite having finished the game as I had the entire soundtrack disabled throughout my entire playthrough and listened to other songs while playing instead. The sound is a different story. First of all - the voice acting. Despite Jess sounding like she's bored 24/7 and Mac getting insanely annoying with how much he just can't shut up about himself, I think the voice acting in this game is pretty good. Characters under their roles sound convincing and there were definitely some moments that had me give the game a chuckle or two.

Optimization wise...well, to preface this - I streamed my entire playthrough of the game on Twitch. And let's just say that my PC isn't the most powerful thing on the planet. So I frequently encountered plenty of stutters, plenty of framedrops and even a few times when the game just unloaded & reloaded everything directly in front of my eyes. Sometimes just not loading ANYTHING at all, causing me to fall through the map! However I'm willing to chalk all that up to just the game struggling to juggle resources on my PC rather than the game itself being very poorly optimized. For the curious - my PC is an i5-4460 with a GTX 1650 and 16GB of RAM.

Also this game REQUIRES Origin. Take that as a warning - [b][u]you will be forced to download and make an Origin account just to play this game.[/u][/b] For some - this might as well be a dealbreaker.

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
Do I recommend NFS Payback? If you want a 10+ hour racing game with callbacks to previous games and a fun handling model, I'd say go for it. At $30 you get your money's worth. If you disliked 2015 like a lot of people did, Payback will make you appreciate the amount of improvements made to basically everything.

However if you don't like engaging with gambling to progress, I'd advise to stay away.

I bought this game expecting it to be another let-down, especially since my previous NFS experiences were Most Wanted (2012) and Rivals, both of which lacked anything substantial and were as hollow as games come. Payback on the other hand proved me wrong and made sure I had a damn good time during the 60 hours that I spent in it. There's a cringeworthy story here but it somehow makes you wanna see it through to the end, and it gives you purpose to upgrade your cars and manage your team throughout different racing disciplines. The opposition gradually becomes stronger and it's up to us to keep up with them.

Performance upgrades aside, the visual ways one can boost their ride are plenty. From bumpers to neons, there's quite a selection of things you can customize, and there really were times when Payback reminded me of the Underground era. It's also got that amazing livery editor where you can use all kinda pictures and shapes to basically paint paintings on your ride. Really loved it.

The handling is very arcadey but it felt much more down-to-earth than, say, NFSMW:2012, especially at lower levels with slower cars. The cars are no longer rockets, they won't automatically start pre-scripted drifting whenever you make a turn, and with a wheel and a sequential shifter the driving actually feels really nice and intuitive. Of course, it's less so when you reach McLarens, Lambos and Koenigseggs, but even they feel good to drive.

Overall, I thought Payback was gonna be a flop NFS game but I had a ball once I started playing. A really well done arcade racer.

That's real stakes, there's a real story here, and you never meet anyone who's just a 1-dimensional douchebag like in so many other titles where they want you to just hate your opponents because they think toxic banter and pure resentment is going to make the races better somehow.

The world isn't full of sore losers whose enormous egos shatter because they lost one race.  Your rivals seem like they're going to just be annoying, then you have conversations with them and you find out their story, and why they hate The House, and then you respect each other after the races are over.  There are some surprisingly nice moments.

The Gambler is an ambiguous character who's really well written, acted and animated, and I'm curious to see what he's going to do.

Your main characters - you drive as three different people - are likeable too.  They care about each other, and they talk about it.  You want them to succeed.

There are a bunch of mechanical problems with the game.  The upgrading system is silly - apparently a different engine head can improve your *checks notes* braking and jumping ability.  It's clearly just there to tie into the weird roulette system that also ties into the microtransation crap.  I know there's a whole gambling subplot but there's nothing that ties them together, I think it was just an excuse to use all the gambling knowledge that you gain working on modern microtransaction hell.  Also some of the open world activities are shallow, like police chases where you have to hit all the checkpoints like it's a timed race, and the cops magically keep respawning until you reach the end where they magically disappear.  It's literally just a checkpoint race where the cops are also there.

And the driving?  It's okay, it's a NFS game, it's arcadey.  It's okay.

But I'm pushing through all that junk because I actually care about the story.

Need for Speed Payback is a strange mix of highs and lows. On the good side, the game nails that adrenaline-pumping sense of speed that the franchise is known for. The car collection is solid, and the drifting feels smooth and genuinely fun once you get the hang of it. Off-roading is surprisingly enjoyable too, and the sound design makes every rev and turbo hiss feel powerful. The various car classes also help keep things fresh, offering distinct experiences depending on what you’re driving.

However, the game leans far too heavily on drift-style racing, with grip-focused driving feeling almost forgotten. Racing an entire circuit with a drag car is more frustrating than fun. The characters don’t help much either. They’re flat, unmemorable, and often annoying. The main character feels one-dimensional, and the “funny” sidekick’s jokes never land. Jess is the only somewhat interesting character thanks to her espionage-style missions, but even she can’t save the story from being painfully bland.

The real dealbreaker, though, is the car upgrading system. Instead of the classic, skill-based customization NFS fans love, Payback forces players into a random lootbox-style system. Upgrades depend on luck rather than effort, making progression feel grindy, repetitive, and blatantly designed for monetization.

In the end, Need for Speed Payback has moments of fun buried under a mountain of poor design choices. A few hours of thrill, but not much else to keep you coming back. Overall rating: 5/10.

[h1]The House always wins…[/h1]
In a world where racing games weren’t striving hard enough to one-up cheesy blockbusters, one franchise steps to the plate, and most notably replaces the word “family” with “crew.” [b][i]Need for Speed: Payback[/i][/b] touts quite the adventurous story, and an expansive scope, but how much of that is any good?

Have to say, Frostbite 3 might not be the smoothest game engine around, but it sure is pretty... sometimes. Garage close-ups of cars and vibrantly lit downtown areas are some of the best views you’ll get in this title, with great shading and model qualities. Compromises are apparent when you look closer to your usually shiny car: reflections are toned down or even absent, no matter if you’ve wrapped your ride in chrome. Daytime looks visually flat despite its vibrant colours. Human animation is a weird mix of bad and good, with nice details but poor posing and timing.

Just one notch below the highest graphical settings, my [i]Ryzen 9 3900X, 64GB RAM, 1070 Ti, Windows 10 Pro[/i] system runs the game at 60fps and 1440p resolution, with occasional dips to the 50s when passing through dark tunnels. Gamepad controls are unrebindable and you have to make do with just two presets… This is how I also realized keyboard controls are rebindable, and not actually bad.

[h3]Air Mac![/h3]
Oh boy, the dialog is just awful. It might’ve banked on the cheesy presentation of mid-2000’s street racing movies, but… come on now. Poor delivery, repetitive self-congratulatory statements from the main characters, forced lines and a generally obnoxious feel to it. Trust me, you’re hardly missing out if you mute it entirely.

Sound design is a little better, thankfully. Aside from being on the quiet side for some reason, even with all sliders at the maximum, you have decent car noises and environmental effects. Finally, music is mostly harmless: a few really good tracks are buried in a sea of generic rap, country and rock. Some standouts are the composed pursuit soundtrack and the Speedcross-exclusive songs. There’s an attempt to reduce repetition by “theming” the score based on time of day and location, but in practice it achieved the opposite.

[h3]-Not bad, Tyler, but you’re still gonna lose.
-I already won. You just don’t know it yet.[/h3]
After a disastrous heist attempt on a high-tech hypercar and the subsequent splitting of his gang, resident boy-racer and self-proclaimed best driver in faux-Las Vegas Tyler Morgan re-assembles his crew with overly-happy British™ person Mac and straight-faced Jess. Helped by a group of slightly less insane characters, one of which being the victim of the prologue’s attempted heist, the protagonists seek out vengeance against the one who sabotaged their heist, and save Fortune Valley from a tyrannical cartel by beating a bunch of gangs at street racing.

A totally ridiculous premise where any genuine tension is broken when racers trash-talk with weak lines such as “gonna CRUSH you”, and totally shattered because the leagues are pretentious butts who are “mistreated and outcast” for literally performing illegal activities.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2869512682
[h3]I see myself… winning it all.[/h3]
At its core, [b][i]Need for Speed: Payback[/i][/b] is a thoroughly arcade-like racer, where the best lines are taken by drifting through corners rather than holding on the edge of grip. This, in itself, is fine. What’s less fine is the handling model’s specific details that undermine this. Instead of throwing your car’s back end out, the handbrake sooner makes you [i]understeer[/i] for a good while. Drifting response, stability and turning circles are, at best, vaguely communicated, and you won’t know if a car is a boat to drive until you invest some good time and money into upgrading and tweaking it. The worst part about this is that the cars generally drive the same, though some weird choices remain dominant over all others – as the likes of 911 RSRs can attest in online play.

Being a modern entry into the franchise, customization and player expression are a big deal. Thankfully you can bet that most every car on display has at least some body parts to pick through. Wider fenders, different rims, a different front and rear end, and a couple generic rear wings with the occasional unique spoiler – not a bad showing. I must give particular praise to the livery editor, which is not only powerful and host to some high-quality wraps, but all can be applied to any car at will. Add some vanity tyre smokes, a lower stance and neon lights, and you can really stand out
[h3]The cards are coming down.[/h3]
Yet while [i]visual[/i] customization is fine, [i]performance[/i] customization is terrible. You have performance cards with specific brands and bonuses attached to them. Buying from in-game stores yields only higher-level cards with barely any bonuses. The ways to get good cards are by either repeatedly grinding out events, or rolling a literal slot machine to get the right combo of stats boosted. Live Tuning, independent of performance cards, makes too little difference towards a better-performing or -driving car.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2869511017
You’ll cover a sprawling map, open for exploration after the prologue with perilous serpentines, wide highways and grid urban layouts. Its size is on the larger side, but you don’t really need even more boring desert to offroad through. Events are split across six different disciplines, which means you’ll have to upgrade at least six different cars, independently of each other. Some discipline-specific gripes include Drag events also including straight-up races and [i]time attacks[/i], in cars that pop wheelies even when stock; and offroad cars are very eager to go airborne and still have an awkward speed limit off the pavement.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2869511562
Meanwhile, another series staple – police pursuits – are sadly locked away in either linear-course events or as part of open-world “bait crates”, where you drive to a nearby destination without getting busted. Their lack of escalation and predictability are a huge shame when considering how solid the pursuit gameplay itself can be. Dodging oncoming Rhinos and shunting cops out of range of their ECMs are a right rush.
[h3]An artist can turn any scrap into a supercar.[/h3]
The main story takes about 20 hours at a leisurely pace, taking you through five chapters and several blockbuster-caliber heists along the way. Past that, exploration is incentivized via collectibles and score-attack sections on the map, which reward cash and rep, and unlock visual customization categories. Rep grants you shipments, from where you unlock vanity customization and get a massive influx of cash and card parts – the Deluxe edition’s free shipments can actually turn the atrocious upgrade system into mere tedium. Meanwhile, beating street leagues gives clues on finding derelicts scattered around the world. Catch ‘em all from generally obvious map indications, and you’ll have another set of free cars to customize and upgrade to your liking. Roaming racers are but a momentary distraction, and finally, multiplayer is actually still alive, if quite limited. Open-world activities generally revolve around simple impromptu drag races with no one bothering to do much else; Speedlists with PvP racing work fine and you can stand a chance to win even against overpowered cars.
[h1]…Well, not tonight, it didn’t.[/h1]
[i]Peak cinematic flair with minimum substance, charm and consistency makes [b]Need for Speed: Payback[/b] difficult to recommend in general; due to its upgrade system, it’s better to avoid entirely.[/i]

[h3]One of Ghost Games' Better Need for Speed Titles.[/h3]

A much improved racing game compared to 2015's effort in pretty much all aspects. Loading is much faster, characters are at least [i]somewhat[/i] likable now, there's a huge variety in main events and side activities, and overall it's simply far more polished. Yes it does have some blemishes here and there and it's also very by-the-numbers, taking a page out of Burnout Paradise's book that popularized this approach to open-world racers, but otherwise  [i]Payback[/i] is a surpisingly robust entry in the franchise. 

For an arcade title the handling model is very competent and further expressed in how the different styles of cars control. This offers a distinct feeling of racing from event to event. Whether you're doing off-road, drag racing, drifting, speed runs or escaping from the cops they all have their own category of eligible cars and make it so there's a high variety in gameplay which forces you to play with multiple vehicles (as opposed to cruising through the campaign with just one that you've tuned up for everything). The only annoyance being that when you are trying to snag up some collectibles on certain terrain your car doesn't handle well you're better off going back to the garage to swap out your ride.  

Speaking of variety, the open-world itself also holds up in this regard what with its sprawling off-road terrain that ranges from lush green backwoods to dusty canyons. There's a city center that's full of casinos and high rises and on the outskirts you've got smaller towns dotted around that evoke pure Americana; all complete with landmarks and places to explore. It's all really well done and give the game an identity and personalty, something that was missing from the 2015 title. That said, there's also vast stretches of desert between all of the main hubs that basically has no points of interest whatsoever so don't go expecting Burnout Paradise or Forza Horizon levels of activity density in that respect. 
 
As far as downsides go is that despite the story and characters being a step up from the previous game (which isn't saying much, admittedly) the voice acting can be [i]very[/i] hit and miss. The same goes for the music choices that feature some of the most milquetoast Indie Blues/Rock imaginable. The type you'd hear in commercials or sizzle reels that aim to be as inoffensive as possible and evoke no feeling whatsoever. You'd argue this is subjective but the entire soundtrack almost sounds like a royalty free affair. Pure background noise. And in a racing game you'd ideally get some blood pumping tracks across all genres but [i]Payback[/i] is extremely lacking here. If EA wanted to cheap out on song licensing then it definitely shows (ironically in the previous game I couldn't actually hear the soundtrack due to a bug but in this one I turned it off myself).  

Another issue I have is that the upgrading system is kind of awkward. Instead of outright buying the parts you want for each category you instead have to contend with a card system that has a certain factor of randomness thrown in as well. It's akin to something like FIFA Ultimate Team and makes actual upgrading an unnecessary hassle. Upon receiving a part (or "speed card") you can then either equip it, send it to your garage, sell it for cash or trade it in and while this does offer some choice I just found it cumbersome at the best of times.  

Otherwise though Payback is a step in the right direction. Yes it's all rather formulaic so your mileage may vary depending on whether or not you have the stomach for yet another open-world racer of this ilk (with a heavy emphasis on story). But for me it's been one of the more enjoyable racing games I've played in the series. The visuals are great, the driving feels good for the most part, and along with the surprisingly solid technical performance it's also been a mostly bug free experience for me as well. 

Considering the fact that this deluxe edition regularly goes on sale for a criminally low 3 Euro (Activision take note) it's been incredible value for money and thus an easy recommend.

Payback is the first NFS game I’ve played and I’m honestly impressed. It was on sale for around €3 and I thought why not give the series a try. It’s hard to make comparisons with other NFS games but perhaps this writing can be helpful for the ones who haven’t given these games a try yet. I’m a fairly casual racing fan who enjoys certain racing games from time to time but I don’t play them a lot. Controlling the cars is typical with differences in feel and strengths based on the stats of a car. A car has 6 equipment slots (turbo, gearbox, head, etc) that can go up to level 18. These slots can be seen as cards where various stats improve. You can upgrade your cars in tune shops. New stock is added every 10 minutes. There are other means to get these cards such as completing story missions and there is kind of a gambling system with a different currency. Then you have 4-6 different car types more suitable for certain missions. See the car types as a job or class system similar to RPG games. The game has 5 main story chapters with lots of missions. There is also plenty of optional content in the form of activities and collectibles (100 chips and 30 billboards). Activities are mini challenges grouped in speed trap, speed run, jump and drift. You need to find them and try to get 3 stars for each one of them. There is more to the game but this is pretty much the main content. 

I didn’t expect the story mode to be this engaging. Sure it’s generic and cliche. I wasn’t interested as much at the beginning but the more I played the more I liked it. It’s mostly thanks to the voice actors. There are many of them and I couldn’t wait to hear what they had to say. Mac is awesome and so is the rest of the crew plus enemies. The game even has a couple of full motion videos and I also wanted more music for being so good. I can imagine there being fears about the economy of upgrading cars and buying them. I vaguely remember complaints about this when the game first released but I didn’t notice anything with this current version. Everything was perfectly balanced and you even get more than you need. I did focus on upgrading one car type and a couple of more for specific achievements. I have around 18+ cars. I’m not into collecting all cars, so it might be different with that in mind. It was such a joy exploring the map, find collectibles, challenges, locations and then continue with the story. The map was the perfect size: not overwhelmingly big and not too small either. Enough to feel like you’re getting lost in your playground but not too much to the point you feel like it’s work and therefore demotivating. The achievements were mostly fine and fair. There are a couple of multiplayer ones though. You can get them quickly as long as you find a team.

In terms of negatives, there are 2 main ones. No extensive filter options when using a map and load times. As mentioned before, the game has many cool things to do. There are many different icons. It’s very odd that there is no option to filter out the activities you’ve completed or the collectibles you’ve found. You have to see them while you’re searching for things you still need to do. The game takes ages to load when you start it, but it also loads often enough in between. It was a bit too much for my liking. Lastly you have to deal with EA’s launcher to play this on Steam but at least it wasn’t a big problem here. All the achievements unlocked without any issues.

Payback felt like an RPG game in a sense. It’s crazy because that’s not what I expected before I got involved. But it’s used in the best way to enhance racing imo. I don’t understand anything about car parts but I got more involved with the way this game simplified and presented this aspect. I wholeheartedly recommend Payback for newcomers, ones who want a casual experience, a fun popcorn ride or completionists who want to get all the achievements. It’s a solid game with a lot to offer (over 61 hours spent). It’s on sale frequently, definitely make use of the offer the next time.

Yes, the upgrading system for cars was a bit tedious but it didn't take much to upgrade things. I also thought the game was very visually good. The graphics and scenery were beautiful.

Need for Speed Payback – Review
The Good
Unlimited Garage Space

A small but very welcome feature. You can collect as many cars as you want without worrying about storage limits, which fits perfectly with a game that encourages experimentation with different builds.

Car Variety

The variety of cars is excellent. There are more vehicles than ever before in the series, covering everything from classic muscle cars to modern supercars. This gives players plenty of options to experiment with different builds and styles.

Customization

The visual customization is one of the strongest aspects of the game. Neon lights return, nitro colors can be changed, tire smoke is customizable, and there are countless body parts available.

Audio

The car audio is phenomenal. Engine sounds are powerful, aggressive, and extremely satisfying to listen to.

It’s easily one of the best sound designs in the entire Need for Speed series.

10/10

Map

The map is huge. Terrain changes a lot depending on location, and the highways are a nice addition.

It is easily one of the best maps in the Need For Speed series.

The day and night cycle is great. Traffic intensity also changes depending on time of day.

There are also nice details like shooting stars at night and planes taking off from the airport during the day.

Good attention to detail.

Snapshot

Snapshot feature is great too.

You can make insane photo shots, especially when you have unlimited car customization options.

AI

I completed the game on Hard difficulty.

The AI is good and challenging.

The Mixed
Performance Customization

Performance upgrades are unfortunately tied to a randomized card system. Instead of simply buying the parts you want, you must spin “tickets” and hope to receive useful upgrades.

On top of that, you receive bonuses only if the cards match the same brand, which adds another unnecessary layer of randomness. This system feels more like a casino mechanic than proper car tuning.

Car types: Drift / Runner / Race / Offroad

I don't like this separation of cars in events.

Why can't I use my car in all events? It is just bad design.

Even if you have the same type of car, sometimes you still can't enter the event and need to buy the same car again, but for a different event type. That makes no sense and feels like the game is forcing you to waste money.

Also, some cars are blocked from certain events completely. And you can't use all cars for a specific event type.

Why?

The Bad
Handling

The handling in this game is worse than in Need For Speed 2015.

At high speed the steering has delay, which makes the cars feel less responsive and sometimes frustrating to control.

The drift system still feels very similar to the previous game. When you press the handbrake the car can suddenly go in a strange direction, which often ruins the driving flow.

Also there is no steering wheel support, even though the previous game had it.

That is not progress. That is a huge step backwards.

Crash cam

This is the worst crash camera I have ever seen in a Need For Speed game.

You can crash at high speed, regain control of the car, and continue driving — but then the screen suddenly fades to black and your car gets reset anyway.

This is extremely annoying because the game interrupts you even when you recover the crash.

There are also spots on the map where you drive slightly off the road and the game instantly respawns you even though you could easily recover.

You can feel this especially during drift events.

Jump locations

Sometimes you try to jump from a mountain to the road below, which should be possible, but the game just respawns you instead.

The game simply does not allow experimentation.

This is just bad design and removes fun moments where players try creative shortcuts.

Heat

There is no police in free roam.

Police chases are only scripted in runner missions, and they feel very repetitive.

Most of the time you just pick up crates and drive to the same destination to escape.

It always feels like driving from point A to point B.

This is disappointing because the map had huge potential for intense police chases with roadblocks and freedom to escape however you want.

Instead we get very limited scripted sequences.

Events

Events like Offroad, Drift, and Runner give very different amounts of money.

The problem appears after finishing the main game.

You end up farming money only on a few events because they pay well.

Most other events become pointless because the rewards are too low.

This hurts replay value.

Glitches on Side Bet

The requirements are bugged when you need to “clean drive” for 80 seconds. You can hit a small bump on an uneven road and the timer resets.

It is not your fault that the suspension touches the ground and you lose all your progress. To complete this side bet you often need to drive very slow — but it’s supposed to be a race.

Near miss requirements are also bad, because you need to be inches from another car. The developers should allow a bigger distance for this challenge.

Many times you think you got a near miss, but the game does not count it. Even when you were already very close to the other car, it still does not register.

Final thoughts

Despite all the bad things, I still enjoyed playing this game.

Need For Speed Payback has a great map, amazing customization, and excellent car sounds.

But many design decisions hold it back especially the random upgrade system, restricted car classes, weak police mechanics, and frustrating crash camera.

The game had the potential to be much better, but several bad design choices prevent it from reaching that level.

Overall: 7/10

Starting with the things I DIDN'T like. And this game has quite a few flaws.

* Always online when it doesn't have to be. The single player campaign has 2 features that require internet connection. Autolog challenges that don't matter since they do not give you literally anything. And community wraps. Don't really need those either.
* Share usage data is on by default. How about no? Shady practices from EA don't surprise anymore, but it doesn't make it right.
* The cutscenes are kinda funny looking. 720p overcompressed and poorly upscaled type of quality.
* Some of the checkpoints are not obvious enough. Had to restart the first speedcross event and watch all of the cutscenes multiple times because of the missed checkpoint. Some checkpoints even in normal city races are small enough to not even cover the whole road. Nitpicking here of course, but come on.
* GPS can be bit broken at times.
* Customisation options are limited and, more importantly, locked behind challenges which makes me want to bother with them even less when I don't give a hoot already.
* To reiterate, watching cutscenes every time you restart an event is not fun and shouldn't be a thing. Just let me skip.
* The game crashed 2 times in 40 hours, which is not too terrible, I guess.
* When you replay events with actual opponents in the race (e.g. race, offroad) they scale based on your car level. And the difficulty, it feels like, gets too steep too quickly. My mismatched 350 build got destroyed by npcs in offroad in particular. A few of the roaming racers have crazy builds-cars-AI too. The game is pretty easy until it suddenly isn't which feels quite jarring. 
* Hated the drift zones. Probably the hardest thing in the entire game. Granted, you don't actually need to do it. Still, the contrast is crazy when you compare it to the campaign and even the other optional challenges. 
* Hated double jumps. This is where you need to jump once, land on another platform and jump again. Stupid mechanic. There were only 2 of those. Should've been none.
* Almost went bald trying to collect the casino chips in the air. Had to use the widest, longest and tallest car I had just to have a chance of hitting these things. I wonder if anyone tested it with anything smaller than Ford F150. Absolutely miserable experience there.
* It also takes the game a surprisingly long time to update the map after the challenge is complete. Maybe to give you time to breathe a little and regain your sanity.
* Didn't really like RACING racing in a drag car. Which is a funny thing because it was pretty easy to beat some of the speed challenges with it later on.
* Drag racing itself feels underutilized. Only 2 chapters, so like, 10 races total. Idk, a wasted opportunity there.
* The game also has no reset button. Don't really know why.
* Gacha system for performance upgrades is better than grinding events until you go mad, true. And you get a lot of free packs anyway. But yeah, their attempt to monetize the game is kind of pathetic. All of the special cars are nonsense. Everything you could buy with real money you shouldn't. 
* And now, the biggest offender of them all. The TRAFFIC!? The game has an absolutely RIDICULOUS number of cars on the roads in free roam. Anywhere too. I can understand it in the city or on a highway. But... Desert roads in the middle of nowhere? Feels like 5 cars on the screen at any given time. Winding mountain roads? Yeah, time to send a GRABAGE TRUCK to the observatory??? Oh and a box truck please! Missing on some supplies or something, smh. Makes completing some of the challenges infuriating. Like WTAF all of these cars are doing there is beyond me. A big oversight from the developers. It gets a bit better at night, but the roads are never empty. The campaign is better though. Free roam traffic is a crime.
* Oh, there are also trucks with ads on them. And billboards too. Shouldn't be a thing in a game you pay money for.




And the things that I enjoyed:
* The the story is pretty engaging and honestly a lot of fun. Overall pretty ridiculous of course, but this hardly matters if it's nice to play; and it is. The intro is longer than I'd prefer though.
* Drifting is still odd, but definitely an improvement compared to the previous title.
* Despite break to drift being a very counterintuitive mechanic it works much better in Payback. There quite a few fast roads that feel rather satisfying to drift on.
* The handling on the whole is a huge improvement. It isn't ideal by any stretch of imagination, but it is better than 2015.
* A lot of different styles of racing. The game actively pushes you to try new things. It can be fun, if a little grindy. Loved the story offroading the most.
* A decent car selection. Great car detail. Maybe a bit of a downgrade compared to 2015. Still looks nice and the game runs better.
* Live tuning exists. TFG!
* Better default key bindings. No page up/down nonsense.
* What's more, you don't have to go to garage to change your car every time you switch between the event types. Just press E to change your car. Getting better and better.
* Limited fast travel that motivates you to drive a little and explore the map to find more fast travel spots and make it even more effective. I'd call it a good balance.
* Had some fun tracking down derelicts. Great mechanic. Ended up abandoning most of my derelict builds in favour of some achievement cars in the end though.
* The music is good. Great stuff for the most part.
* Good attention to details. The character moves when turning the wheel and looks back when reversing. Loved that.
* There is a night/day cycle, which is honestly pretty impressive. The skybox is dynamic and you can see the stars moving at night. Really impressed by it.
* Another interesting bit is that cars get dirty when you drive them offroad. 
* The damage model is purely cosmetic, but looks pretty cool IMO. Glass breaks, metal bends, plastic cracks. Good stuff.
* The crashes are much less annoying than in 2015. Much harder to actually crash out too.
* Loved racing different crews, loved the throwbacks.
* Challenging roaming racers should've been a reward based system. Gives you absolutely nothing other than the achievement. Well, and the unique dialogue. Still had good time doing most of these. 
* The dialogue is nice too. Feels natural enough to me. Obviously corny and silly sometimes, but good.
* A lot of unique npcs with personalities and all. Annoying too. I am talking about you Natalia!
* You can in fact fast travel somewhere and the game will automatically pause the call and continue playing afterwards. Talking real QOL here. It will cancel if you enter events/garage though.
* Had a blast 'playing' different characters too. I personally found it very fresh after being 'yourself' or a random faceless dude in all? of the previous titles. Each with their unique personality and dialogue and stuff. Great addition.
* Unlimited car storage is great. And the game is pretty generous with money so you can try out new cars much easier.
* I kind of liked the bait crate mechanic. Allows you to interact with the police at least somewhere outside the story and gives you an alternative to farming events for parts. Win-win in my book.
* I think that the performance upgrade system is fine. You have multiple ways to get the parts. It gives you a reason to replay the events, other than just to get money. Can't be mad at that. Not a big fan of the lottery side of it, but hey.

Overall, a huge improvement over 2015. Will probably return one day to replay the story.

[h1] Introduction[/h1]
Ghost Games third entry in the series. At the time, hyped during the E3 reveal for its graphics and story missions. Need For Speed: Payback was welcomed at first as one of the series most lackluster games, and is generally branded as an easy pass when it comes to racing games. Yet here am I, giving a postive review. And trust me, I'm not gonna tell you "oh no this game is misunderstood, it's actually a masterpiece!". But allow me to explain some things:

[h1] Cars[/h1]
When it comes to cars, how is Payback's roster? While it certainly isn't as overreaching as Heat's roster, it's actually in a very nice middle ground. Payback is currently the only game in the series which allows you to build a car from derelict parts, and this feature allowed the introduction of some rare, but interesting cars, such as the Chevrolet Bel Air, or the Volkswagen Beetle. Said feature also allowed for an interesting feature - as these cars aren't just for show. You can literally build late game killers from these cars. And while irrealistic, I'll admit it was one of the fun parts ("bye Lambo, eat my '65 Mustang dust"). 

Regarding other cars, the roster is comprised from oldies like Volvo 242, to JDMs such as the Silvia and the RX-7, to a very beautiful selection of hypercars, from the Viper to a wide selection of Lambos and Porsches, and an appearence by the mighty Regera. Beware tho - money doesn't grow in trees in NFS: Payback, so invest your money and time carefully in your rides.

[h1] Gameplay[/h1]
[u] Soundtrack[/u]: soundtracks often come as a winning point in NFS games. Most Wanted and Underground 2 are still games which made certain songs be stuff of legends. Even Hot Pursuit is and was widely aclaimed for its soundtrack. Payback tho... Eh. It's in a weird mixture of trap/hip hop to a certain type of electronic which doesn't sit well with the environment at all. I enjoyed about 50% of the songs, to be gentle.

[u] Race types[/u]: 10 points for Team Payback here. Race types are most fun and varied, and Drag races are incorporated again in the storyline. While pursuit mode is a bit lackluster here, Runner missions are actually some of the most fun I've had, and they're a good mix of "mission" and "pursuit".

[u] Environment/Aesthetic[/u]: not the prettiest in its class. Heat and 2015 are the definitive experience if you play Need For Speed for the aesthetics. However... that doesn't mean Payback is ugly or anything. Snapshot Pro is actually a nice upgrade from 2015, and I've actually taken some nice pics from the game.

[u] Fortune Valley[/u]: not the best map. At all. Underground 2's map is retirement-old as of this time, and the highways, road mountains and side alleys make up for a better ride than Fortune Valley. The redeeming feature is the off-road part, where offtrack you can actually get a fun experience out of cruising.

[u] Performance parts[/u]: ugh. No. No. Never again. Payback is the ONLY entry so far where performance upgrades are done thru "Speed Cards", which you get in a "surprise mechanic", EA-type of lootbox kind of thing. Again - there's a reason why this is the ONLY entry where this happens. The community came down on this game over it.

After all this, why is my review positive?

[u] Gameplay[/u]: Story-wise, it's uninspired (I don't wanna spoil it for anyone, but ugh. Seriously. Wanna play NFS for the story? Skip this one). But the way the game feels? Oof. I've drifted with an offroad-prepped '65 Mustang in the middle of the mountains. I took my RSR to unmatchable speeds through the mountains tunnels. I drifted in the middle of the forests with a BMW M4 GTS like I was DK himself. I damaged police cars doing Neville's move in Need For Speed: Carbon with a monster of a Camaro. While the brake-to-drift configuration was appaling to many, Payback will be worthwile to the casual, day-to-day Need For Speed player.
This game has the best map ( except it was way to restricted for an open world game ) and best handling model compared to recent NFS games. Use *Unite* mod for better experience. 5/10
